chunks.text: We're ready to get underway, and we have further hearings on the Social Security Amendment Bill. And the first submitter we have this afternoon is Good Shepherd New Zealand. We have Good Shepherd New Zealand online. Bree, over- Kia ora Oh, kia ora. Welcome. All right. We have 10 minutes with you this afternoon. The time is yours when you're ready to go.

Thank you, and thank you for the opportunity to speak today. I'm the policy lead for Good Shepherd New Zealand. We are a charitable NGO focused on two of the biggest issues facing women and girls, in particular in New Zealand, being poverty and family violence, and the challenges that stem from these. First, I'll speak to the policy tightening eligibility criteria for jobseeker support. So as noted in MSD's own RIS, the benefits for young people of these changes are likely to be significantly outweighed by the costs, and we're really concerned about the further hardship that

this may create for households. We do understand the need to target funding towards those who most need it. But as the cost of living has risen, New Zealand has seen more poverty and more of the squeezed middle, lower to middle-income households who are struggling to make ends meet. There is a serious risk that many families will not be able to financially support their children past their school years.

As New Zealand is already experiencing high and unmoving child poverty rates due to the financial pressures on households with children, these households are also facing rising energy costs and food prices increasing, amongst other things. Stagnant incomes at the moment are not sufficient to meet these costs. The Helen Clark Foundation's recent report on social cohesion found that one in four New Zealand households go without meals because they can't afford food, and the clients that we serve report similar activity.

The parental income limit in this policy, which is around $65,000 to $67,000, is much lower than the annual gross household income, which is currently sitting at around $139,000, and also lower than some other parental income tests that we see for payments, such as the student allowance, which is around $101,000 if you live with your parents. It's currently unclear how family size and other dependents will be taken into consideration here. What is clear is that young people whose parents earn over this threshold but who will not or cannot support

them will be left behind. Rainbow youth and those experiencing family violence will likely be over-represented in this group, especially where estrangement is difficult to prove. We note that the first two objectives in this policy, as noted in the bill, center on fiscal sustainability and incentivizing youth to enter work. But making it harder for young people to access the jobseeker benefit will not incentivize them to enter a job market if there are no jobs to hire them.

The recent 2026 Salvation Army State of the Nation report states that over a quarter of a million people are currently wanting work but are unable to find it. That challenge is very real. The entry-level job market in particular is challenged due to the rise of AI, the global economic context, and many young people are applying for hundreds of jobs without success. Under this policy, young people will also miss out on some of the coaching and support that are offered by case managers through the jobseeker benefit that might really be able to help them when applying for those roles.

We think that government policy should focus on investing in labor market stimulus, increasing business activity, opportunities, and education. MSD's original preferred option was to provide a range of targeted employment and changing programs which predicted savings in the long term through lower future benefit levels. We do know that Budget 2026 has promised an extra thousand Youth Guarantee places, which is great.

But given the policy in this bill is estimated to impact over 4,000 young people, there is a significant gap here. We also know that unfortunately, many of the young people who are currently struggling to find work are university graduates already, showing that education alone is not currently sufficient to pull youth out of unemployment. The job market needs to be stimulated as well to provide new opportunities for those who are exiting tertiary education.

People also need funds to enable employment opportunities. Young people who are denied benefits and have no money to buy a car cannot travel to a job if public transport options don't exist. They can't afford appropriate work wear for a job interview or buy tools needed for their trade. They cannot pay for that additional training that could support them into work. While the majority of the loans that we provide, so no interest, no fee loans for people under a certain income threshold, they're usually for things like a car or debt consolidation, we do also provide loans for

educational or training-related expenses or technology like laptops to enable study. There is a need for these things. If parents are forced to become financially responsible for their children for longer, it's also likely that there'll be an increase in demand for assistance provided by NGOs or charities like ourselves or food banks.

For example, the Zero Hunger Collective here at Kaikoore reports an increase in two-income households who are visiting food banks across the country. This is expected to only worsen. So that's in work poverty in action. Charities and social services fill a really needed gap in responses to poverty, but many have been forced to close down due to funding cuts or contracts not being renewed.

The charitable sector can't be the ambulance at the bottom of the cliff, and we're not going to succeed if there aren't contracts to fund them to do so. I'll now move on to the second proposal in the Bill, changing the entry threshold for the accommodation supplement. We note that housing makes up a significant portion of financial pressure for many households. Housing tends to be a fixed household cost, so that's unable to be reduced or budgeted around.

While the majority of our clients are in rental or some form of social housing, around 13% live in a home that they own themselves. So this shows that despite owning their house, these clients are under enough financial pressure to need to come to us to be able to purchase those essential goods and services such as whiteware, for example. Now, there is a number of reasons why people who own homes may be experiencing financial stress.

Even though we have seen some house price trend improvement and some shifts in the affordability criteria, which is fantastic, those who bought homes at record highs or are locked in those higher interest rates will continue to struggle. Local government rates across the country are also set to increase 5% to 10% in the coming year. High numbers of redundancies across all sectors, public, private, and social sector, seriously reduce household incomes, especially in this really tough job market we're currently in, where unemployment might be extended.

Divorce or separation can result in one person taking over a mortgage unexpectedly, and this is particularly challenging when family violence is involved. Both situations disproportionately impact women's financial wellbeing. Simply stating that the accommodation supplement exists to help homeowners accumulate a personal asset ignores the current state of the economy and the variable housing market.

I'll share a quick example of a Good Shepherd client who I'll call Lillian. Lillian had experienced family violence in her relationship with her ex-husband. When he left, she suddenly found herself to be a solo mum living in the house that they legally co-owned together, but he'd stopped paying the mortgage, maintenance for the house, any other bills.

The washing machine broke, the shower leaked, but she couldn't afford to fix them. While trying to get her life back together after abuse, she had to navigate paying these bills alone on a limited budget. With our help, she was eventually supported into financial stability, but this example shows some of the complexity of homeowner situations and how it's often a lot more complicated than that.

So if this Bill goes through, we do really strongly support the exclusions that are noted, especially for superannuants. Our own research into single older women's housing needs has shown that many older people who own their home do not experience affordable, warm housing. Poor housing quality, particularly for older homes that were purchased potentially many decades ago, combined with rising rates and insurance costs, put significant pressure on superannuant homeowners who lack the ability to generate additional income. Just another client example I'll share.

We have recently supported an 80-year-old woman living in rural South Island, so the deep south. Her house was purchased many decades ago, and she couldn't afford to upkeep it. Her health was really suffering because the heating was completely inadequate during the freezing winters. Her family lived far away, and she was reliant completely on the super. Her budget was really tight, and she couldn't afford to buy a heat pump. So we were able to support her by providing a grant, and we've helped many others like her with this kind of essential home maintenance

needs. But this shows how older people are desperately in need of any dollar that they are able to get, especially because they can't earn the additional income. So overall, we are disappointed to see another policy progressing that's focused on these short-term financial savings instead of long-term outcomes. We believe that kicking the can down the road does not support financial sustainability in the long run.

It just creates false economies, and we need to take a long-term lens. Thank you for your time. Thank you. Any questions, members? Francesca. Thank you, and a very comprehensive submission from Good Shepherd. I'm interested in what you said earlier about the struggle for young people to find work and employment opportunities.

Can you elaborate on what you're seeing on the ground? Yeah. Partly it's hard because we're a small service, so unfortunately, we can't support everybody. What we see a lot of the time is people who come to us who don't meet affordability criteria, and that's the hardest thing, is having to turn people away because legally, we can't put people into further hardship. But, yeah, we're seeing a lot of people doing it tough at the moment, and I think it's going to get harder if the job market, in particular, doesn't improve.

Thank you. All right. Thank you for coming and making a submission this afternoon. Thank you for the written submission as well. Kia ora. Thank you. All right. Our next submitter is the Manuel Poe Family Whānau Trust.

Hello again, Frances. Now, I see you've- From-... basically put the same submission as I had the committee yesterday on a different bill. I'll just make a couple of quick comments before you get underway. Section 25 of the Crimes Act, I've been a lawyer and worked in the courts all across New Zealand. That is regards to crimes. The government establishes the law, so that's not relevant to this committee's consideration of this bill.

And, the New Zealand government is not registered under the foreign government of the US Securities and Exchanges Commission, so that's not relevant either. But look, if you- The New Zealand government isn't- Correct. But if you want to make submissions that are relevant- Under the US securities... if you want to make submissions that are relevant to this bill, I'm happy to hear that, but I would ask you to make submissions that are relevant to the bill that we're considering.

So you aren't ignorant to the law then? No, we make the law. So we're interested in hearing your submissions on the- So you do know about the law, right? On the bill that we're considering. Okay. All right. So, kia ora koutou. This is a demand on request under urgency, a notification of a cease and desist under the official complaints, and a demand on request, a independent internal investigation into the Social Security bill.

This is against the Coalition Government Select Committee, House of Representatives, and the Governor General, identifying any unusual legislative features of this bill. This bill is flawed. We do not give consent to any ADM or Social Security bill at this time. It fails to comply with the treaty principles. It fails to comply to the Privacy Act 2020. It fails to comply to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. Failing to comply to the Public Service Act 2020. Request for all private and financial information concerning the Social Security bill.

Certification and accreditation process to give a provided the safeguard for any use of ADM. Does these safeguards have unintended bias, or discrimination against Māori or other groups, cultures, or other forms of disabilities? Is it in compliance with the principles of the treaty, and does it follow the Bill of Rights Act?

Note that one of the requirements under the ADM standards is that where unintended bias cannot be removed or significantly mitigated from a ADM process, human involvement must be in process at all times, or decisions will be made by human involvement, which would then mean that the decision is no longer an automated decision.

Automated decision- Sorry, Frances. Can I just pause you there for a moment? This bill is not considering automated decision-making. This bill- So it's not in there? I think you're thinking of a separate bill. There was one, but- There was one previously, but that's not this one. It's not this one? No, correct. Okay. Does the department have a disclosure statement?

Has the MSD prepared a disclosure statement concerning any access information to the scrutiny of this bill? Does this bill consist with the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi? Has the government engaged with Māori? Has the government consulted with Māori?

Under the privacy and standards of the New Zealand Bill of Rights, has the government complied to the rules, regulations, legislations, under their responsibilities, obligations, and duties? Under the coalition government, within three years, the government has put New Zealand citizens and Māori into a financial economic crisis, bringing harm to the most vulnerable.

We have the highest rates of unemployment, homelessness, crime, incarceration, business liquidations, mortgagee sales, rises in cost of living, food, gas, water, rent, medical cost, and power. Shortage of disability services, public services, government-funded services. Nurses, doctors, not enough funding.
Teachers, police, fire, ambulance, not enough funding. How has the government made provisions for our most vulnerable?

The government, with this bill, along with other bills they have submitted and created to harm public, has caused public scrutiny and unrest due to the intentional, deliberate action of the coalition benefiting from the corporation as a corporate entity.

No, it- Bringing harm and poverty and financial economic crisis, attacking our most vulnerable through these bills. A demand and request for all official financial private information concerning the Social Security bill. Why is this bill targeting our most vulnerable?

How have they made- Provisions for our most vulnerable. Does the government have any plans of stopping the financial economic crisis that we are facing today as New Zealand citizens and Māori? The Manuel Pou Family Whānau Trust demand on request under urgency an official complaint, a notification of a cease and desist, an independent internal investigation, and official information into this

bill for the suppression, oppression, persecution against the most vulnerable Māori, the disabled, the poor of New Zealand. And we wish you, government and select committee, to answer these questions, please.

Thank you. All right. Thank you, Frances. Any questions for Frances Manners? No, thank you. Yeah. Willie. Frances, just explain to us about the treaty principles. How do you see the treaty principles being breached? So with the treaty principles, when it comes to Māori, we have self-management rights to control our own resources and our own affairs.

Also, under Kāwanatanga, we recognize under Crown that the government is to make laws for the country, which is fair and just. We all must be treated equally, ensure that all New Zealand citizens are equal before the law, and we must have reasonable cooperation, requires both parties to act in good faith and engage in fair consultation. And also, we must have the right to redress, impose

any obligations on the Crown to provide process of resolving any grievances and past breaches to our treaty partnership. Kia ora, Frances. Thanks for making a submission this afternoon. Make a lot of sense to me, Frances. Thank you very much.

All right. Ka pai. Getting my questions off I don't think you had any more questions. Ka pai. Thank you, Frances. Well done. Keep it up. So you buy the argument, do you, Willie? I really agree with that we're all equal before the law. I agree with that. Agree we're all equal, absolutely.

We're all equal before the law. All right. Now, next submitter is a Māori woman- And Māori have special set of rights, as you well know... Māori Women's Welfare League. Oh, ask me that question as well, will you? Do it just for New Zealand first. All right. Well, welcome. We have 10 minutes with you this afternoon. Welcome. Kia ora.

Kia ora. Kia ora. Kia ora. My name is Hope Tupara, and I'm the national president of the Māori Women's Welfare League. Thank you for-- You've read my written submission, ka pai. This bill is dumb. And it's dumb because it isn't going to save money.

It's going to cause more costs down the track. Most of our kids get on okay. Even kids that are studying now or working, they're still struggling. We've got lots of young ones struggling. So we reject this bill, and we think you should reject it as well.

Because you're targeting vulnerable young people who are struggling more than their peers. Can't get jobs. Typically, Māori kids leave school a bit earlier than their peers. We also know that Māori women tend to have babies younger, so they're going to end up-- And we have a lot of single Māori women looking after their children. So that means they're going to have teenagers a lot sooner than some of their other women.

And we've got a lot of generations living in one house, not just Māori either. A lot of Pākehas are living with lots of generations in their house to cope because of homelessness, because they don't want to be homeless. I was just talking to one the other day, a Pākeha woman who's got young people, lots of generations living in her house because that's how they're trying to cope.

Now, when you've got lots of generations, it causes a lot of stress, as you probably know. If you've got children, grandparents. Because our homes now are not designed like marae for lots of people living under one roof. So you're going to naturally have a lot of stress. Now, most of the people in this room have benefited from past policies of government, where there were lots of jobs.

You could go from one job to another. There was a lot of money in education, and so I benefited from that in tertiary. A lot of us did. But we are imposing on young people a set of conditions today that none of us, well, a lot of us in this room, didn't have to go through. But they are going through. But I ask you, why?

Why are we targeting our young people? Why are we doing this to them? They are going to be the workforce of the future. And we've taken away student loans. We put more penalizing young people. We've done lots of things to young people, and I don't get it.

I don't understand why we're doing that to young people when many of us have not had those conditions in which we grew up and went into work. So I ask you, for a lot of reasons, that a lot of the submitters have already talked about. You're not going to save money. It's going to hit you down the track.

You're impacting people who are already vulnerable. You're impacting people who are actually doing okay, but just surviving. Young people, it's a special thing to want to have independence. We've all been there. You know what it feels like when you've had enough of living under somebody's roof with somebody else's rules, and you need your own space.

And I'm not talking about people who have got no choice. I'm talking about people who actually got a choice, but actually you're limiting some of the choices for many of our young people. So you need to throw this bill out. And like she said, it's a breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

And the reason it's a breach is because I want to know how many people, how many of you have actually gone into the communities and sought solutions in partnership with our hapū and iwi. Because I know that it's affecting mostly Māori. This bill is going to affect mostly Māori youth. And if you want to work in partnership, you want to work under Te Tiriti, then go and see the people on the ground and ask them for the solutions.

That's where they are. Not in this whare. Anyway, that's me. I've had enough. Sorry. Thank you. I want to just make a couple of comments and then a sort of question. Yes. Because I'm not one of those who benefited. I'm a kid. No, a bit later. I'm a kid- Yes... in the '80s and '90s who-... especially the '80s, had no food on the table.

And had to work really hard to get out of poverty. And also, didn't get anything free. The university, I had to pay for all that. Well, not didn't have to pay for it because the government actually pays 85% roughly of university. And none of these kids now actually want to be on the benefit. Yeah, and that's coming to my question.

Because this is targeting 18 to 19-year-olds who are sort of in that really important transition between family, the family home, school, often, and the rest of their lives. And so this is a really important, I think you want to hear a few things, a really important part of their lives, and we want to encourage them to either employment or education or training. Because it is- That doesn't exist, and you know it.

You know that the NEET rates have gone up, and you know that unemployment's gone up in the last quarter. So the conditions that you're talking about don't actually exist like they used to. Even in your time, they were better than they are now. They were. I'm not sure about that, to be fair, but the- No, I'm sure about it.

Would you agree that it'd be better for young people to be in training or study if they're not in employment, to ultimately upskill and to help get them ready for employment? I don't think it's available everywhere, though. Even though you have training programs around the country, it's not necessarily available everywhere.

And in the rural areas, sometimes it's actually harder because you don't have access to public transport like you might do in the cities. I don't know if it's easier in the cities, to be honest. But in many families, they might have just the one car. It's a bit harder now with petrol costs.

And so you're kind of reliant on somebody taking you in their car or public transport to get to training. Mm. So, I mean, other submitters have probably canvassed a lot of the issues that come up. But in rural areas, so I live in a kind of a rural area.

Mm. But we have very limited public transport. There are some training centers in the area, but they usually are quite specific courses. Yeah. I grew up in a rural area. Yeah. And still live in one now. Willie. Can I just ask, with the Māori Women's Welfare, this is a kaupapa being traversed amongst all our women, is it?

This- Yeah. Well, because our branches, we've got 160 branches across the country. Yeah. And they're on the ground. Mm. So, they've got firsthand contact with a lot of our young people anyway. Apart from their own, there's other young people that are in the community.

Yeah. And they're not necessarily just Māori either. No. Because they might be their friends, too. I know. And also, yes and no. I mean, you guys were having some love affair with Winston there for a while. And so he can, just for David's information, he might not know that he- Know all about that, my friend. And so him and Shane, they'd be backing you on this, wouldn't they?

Well, I would like to hope so. Yeah. I would've thought that was- Are you New Zealand First? Oh, yes. Oh, yes. Are you? We love your work. Yeah, they love your work. Do you love what I just said? No, probably not. Parts of it. Okay. But I would say that I've worked with your mate Honi up north, as an example. And on the ground looking at ways to create employment and usually with hapū and with iwi. To me, that's kind of a way forward, but it's not asking you a question because that's my job.

I'm meant to be asking you a question. I see the question was- Helen. Helen. No. You said that we were going to pay for this later And so I'd like to know about that. My second question, so you can choose really, because we haven't got much time, but is what about the pressure on those parents that you were talking about. Those parents, we need more kids in this country.

Yeah. We're about to load on parents of 18-year-olds a whole bunch more- Mm... financial pressure. Exactly. What was your first question? The first question, what are the consequences that you spoke of? Oh. Well, just imagine. Mental health problems comes to mind straight away.

Mm. Because it's a stressful time being a teenager. There's a lot of hormones going on. There's a lot of stress, a lot of pressure. Your parents want you to do this, they want you to do that. Your peers want you to do this, they want you to do that. But also you internally want things for yourself as well. And if you can't get them, that would be psychologically damaging.

Mm. And then that would lead to all sorts of physical ailments. So health is the immediate one that comes to mind. And then, if you get into desperation, you might go down a bad track, maybe even commit crime because you've got no other choice.

Oh. So that's another pipeline, isn't it? It's a potential pipeline. A job is good. A job is good if you get a job. Yeah. You need somebody who actually will employ you. And these days, it's usually someone that knows you. If you're a young Maori kid, you're probably less likely to be employed.

That's a fact. Oh, thank you, Dr. Hope. Appreciate you coming in and making a submission. Thank you. And thank you for leaving us time for questions as well. I really appreciate it. No worries. Thank you. The next submitter is, Parents of Vision Impaired NZ via Zoom.

Good evening, Dr. Rebecca. Welcome. Kia ora. Lovely to be here. Nice to see you all again. Likewise. All right. The time is yours when you're ready. Lovely. So I'm here on behalf of Parents of Vision Impaired New Zealand. PVI supports the goal of enabling young people to participate in education, employment, and community life.

However, we are concerned that this bill moves in the opposite direction for our disabled young people by increasing barriers to income support without addressing the barriers that prevent their participation in the first place. I didn't cover in my written submission about why a disabled young person might receive job seeker support, either job seeker support or job seeker health and disability rather than supported living payment. And I just wanted to cover that briefly, because our parents tell us that the SLP is

extremely difficult to obtain for the young person. It requires extensive administration work and a raft of documentation. And the SLP does have a carve-out for totally blind persons, but not all of our vision-impaired young persons are totally blind. So that creates a challenge. What it means is that sometimes disabled young people receive job seeker because they do not meet the current eligibility criteria for supported living. It has a higher threshold based on the impact of disability on a person's ability to work or sustain employment.

Young people may also have some potential work capacity, even though meaningful employment can be difficult to access without significant support. Also, transitioning from school is complex. While its supports may exist on paper, we call these supports as imagined, rather than supports as they exist.

Our parents talk about the transition cliff after school. They talk about transitioning to what. There's very little for our young persons to transition into, particularly as it relates to vision-related disabilities, because they impact so much on young people's ability to engage in education, their employment prospects, daily living, and ability to navigate the labor market.

As I mentioned, barriers to employment include inaccessible workplaces, lack of transport options, employer attitudes, the need for workplace accommodations, limited availability of specialist employment support, and disrupted education pathways. Job seeker can act as a stabilizing support during this transition period while a young person recovers from schooling. And I'd note there that vision does create an extra challenge and does exhaust our young people sometimes.

So sometimes they need a bit of time to recover as they prepare to seek further employment and training. This gives them time to explore rehabilitation options, disability-related supports, and explore part-time study options. And this is where the other stuff gets interesting, because part-time study isn't as well-supported as full-time study, and it can be really difficult to navigate this financially. And so our concern is that this bill creates barriers to financial support without addressing the underlying challenges, and instead increases financial hardship and

makes it harder to achieve independence. The bill does assume that family support is available. But as I'm sure you're aware from the stats around disability, households with a disabled person, including a disabled child, have consistently higher rates of material hardship than households without.

Families with a disabled child are more likely to experience material deprivation, more likely to experience financial stress, more likely to report unmet health and disability-related needs, and disability in childhood is associated with higher household costs, reduced parental employment, and a higher likelihood of living in an income-poor household.

This means that these households are less able to provide financial support when a child turns 18. For our young people, turning 18 does not necessarily represent the transition into independence in the way this policy assumes. Instead, it's actually a transition period where they need more support.

More support to navigate the options, more support to navigate employment or further education, more support to understand disability services and adult systems. For our young people, income support is the foundation that allows them to participate. It helps with things like the additional cost of transport, which is increasing due to the cuts to total mobility.

It helps with the support and assistive technology. As some of you would have heard during the submissions on the DSS bill, some of these costs are not adequately covered by DSS. If they want to undertake volunteer work or to explore that kind of volunteer options in terms of what could work, that comes with costs.

So reducing access to income support before employment barriers are addressed makes the pathway into employment harder, not easier. And lastly, we're also concerned about the proposed changes around the accommodation supplement, and that is because of those income-related challenges, and it's really important, particularly when you have a disabled child, that you have stability and accessibility and continuity of care.

And so that accommodation support can help those households to retain that stability. And I'm going to stop there because that gives you time. Oh, we recommend rejection of the bill and removing or revising parental income testing, particularly as it relates to a disabled child.

We'd also like to see disability impact analysis done in regard to welfare reforms prior to coming to select committee. So yeah, time for questions. All right. Thanks, Rebecca. Questions, members? David. Thank you very much, Rebecca. I've worked with a lovely lady called Minnie Barr-Guinath for a number of years. She's on the board.

And you'll know her well. One of the issues that we confronted quite regularly was that there's a lack of understanding in the workplace about what people with vision impairments can offer and how easy it is. Is that a real pinch point for your organization and the people that you serve?

Yeah. Yeah, it is. It's hard because our young people don't... I don't want to say they don't know how to advocate. They do. But some of that is learning that occurs over time. So adults often have had a bit more experience in that, whereas an 18-year-old's still navigating the world as a newly minted adult and trying to figure this stuff out.

And the barriers they face, you're young, and you have a vision impairment, and you may not know what supports are available or how to access the supports. And some of those supports exist on paper, but if, A, if you're not aware of them, but B, if you don't know how to access them, they might as well not exist. So that's a real challenge, too, is trying to keep our young people informed as to what supports exist out there and how they can go about navigating that space.

So Rebecca, I'm actually asking about the employer side. Oh, sorry. Yeah. So, they just don't know how or what they're dealing with and- Yeah... aware. Yeah. Yeah. And I can understand, too, employers, they want someone who can do the job, and they're often really reluctant because they don't know if this person can do the job and they're there, they've got a particular goal in mind, and they're not a social service. And there's a real tension there around how do we support employers because they don't know how to...

They're quite-- I don't think they mean to be discriminatory, but they're often quite discriminatory. Not all. Then I've got a-- It's almost like a sub my question. We've heard a lot about people who, they don't want to go into more study. They want to work, and they apply and apply and apply, and they can't get it. And we've heard people say that often the only way they get a job is because they've got a friend or there's a contact. Do you see that when it comes to young people with disabilities, that- Oh-... they get the jobs through friends?

Absolutely. Absolutely. There's a young man, I won't share the name because obviously we're here. But he's phenomenal. He's incredibly capable. Totally blind, uses braille. A very, very competent young man. Can't get work. The only work he get-- Even with the supports that are available, they offered him very menial labor, even though he's a very capable, competent, intelligent young man.

They saw his disability and automatically sort of sent him into very menial work, and he's like, "Well, actually, I do want to go to university. I'm just not ready straight after school, and I want to work in a field that's related to what I want to study and what I'm interested in." And yet he couldn't even get that sort of volunteer intern unpaid type situation because of the nature of his disability. It's heartbreaking.

Yeah, thanks And frustrating because it's- Yeah... untapped potential. Yeah. That's all right. All right, thank you very much, Rebecca, for coming and making the submission this afternoon. Thank you very much. And thanks for Riddles' submission as well. Our next minute is- Just apologies, you go to minister. Okay, all right.
